name: EverCrypt (HACL*) Curve25519 (Vale-optimized)
workload: Curve25519 scalar multiplication (the ECDH key exchange used in TLS 1.3), cycle count per operation, measured with a Linux kernel crypto benchmarking suite
claimed_speedup: EverCrypt's targeted (Vale-assembly) Curve25519 implementation narrowly exceeds OpenSSL's by ~3% (also ~1% faster than Oliveira et al.'s hand-written asm and ~22% faster than Erbsen et al./fiat-crypto's verified C)
benchmark_url: https://project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf (Figure 9, 'EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider', IEEE S&P 2020)
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; EverCrypt/HACL* code is used in Firefox NSS and other Project Everest artifacts
tradeoffs: Source is written in F*/Low*/Vale and compiled via KaRaMeL to C/assembly rather than hand-written C; gains formal proofs of memory safety, functional correctness and secret-independence (constant-time) at the cost of a heavy build toolchain (F*, KaRaMeL, Vale) compared to a plain C/asm library.
caveats: The paper's headline claim is mostly 'matches or exceeds' OpenSSL rather than a large win — the concrete beat documented with full methodology is only ~3% on this one primitive (Curve25519) on one 2017-era CPU. The same paper's AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305 figures (Figs. 7-8, i9-9900K) show EverCrypt's targeted implementation roughly matching OpenSSL's rather than clearly beating it, so do not extrapolate the 3% figure to other primitives. The actively-maintained home for production use has since moved to https://github.com/cryspen/hacl-packages.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: HACL* GitHub README citation trail to the EverCrypt IEEE S&P'20 paper PDF (project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf), located after arXiv queries for 'verified cryptographic OpenSSL performance' surfaced only related/adjacent papers

name: picotls "fusion" AES-GCM engine
workload: AES-256-GCM AEAD encryption throughput for QUIC-sized short blocks (1440 bytes) compared to 16KB blocks
claimed_speedup: OpenSSL's AEAD throughput drops ~30% when encrypting 1440-byte blocks vs. 16KB blocks; picotls's 'fusion' engine cuts that short-block penalty to ~10% (derived from page data), i.e. fusion is meaningfully faster than OpenSSL specifically on QUIC-sized AEAD blocks
stars_or_usage: 641 stars; used in the H2O HTTP server
tradeoffs: Fusion is x86-64-specific and written in plain C (not hand assembly) to keep pipelines full for short AEAD blocks; it's one of four interchangeable crypto backends in picotls (OpenSSL, minicrypto, fusion, libaegis), so using it is opt-in and the OpenSSL backend remains the default for portability.
caveats: No CPU model or compiler flags are stated in the PR description, so this is capped at tier C rather than A/B. The chart gives only relative overhead percentages (not raw cycles/byte), and the OpenSSL version referenced (1.1.1g) is now several releases old.
found_via: GitHub README read for h2o/picotls, then opening its merged PR #310 ('"fusion" AES-GCM engine') which contains the benchmark writeup and graph

name: Tempesta TLS (in-kernel TLS handshakes)
workload: Server-side full and abbreviated TLS 1.2 handshakes (ECDHE+ECDSA over NIST P-256), measured with the tls-perf tool, and full HTTPS transactions measured with wrk, comparing in-kernel Tempesta TLS handshakes against Nginx 1.19.1 + OpenSSL 1.1.1d on a 1-vCPU KVM VM (host: Intel Core i7-6500U) and on 2 bare-metal Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 servers
claimed_speedup: 40-80% more TLS connections/sec than Nginx/OpenSSL and up to 4x lower average/95th-percentile latency in the VM and bare-metal session-resumption cases; but only +6% handshake throughput for new sessions on bare metal, where Nginx/OpenSSL actually has 50-170% lower average/95th-percentile latency and Tempesta's worst-case tail latency is up to ~30x higher
hardware: 1-vCPU KVM VM on host Intel Core i7-6500U (no vAPIC); 2x bare-metal Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 with Mellanox ConnectX-2 10Gbps NICs
is_fork_of: https://github.com/ARMmbed/mbedtls (originally forked from mbed TLS 2.8.0; the paper states only PKI code remains from the original mbed TLS source, with a full rework of handshake, crypto and memory handling)
tradeoffs: Linux-kernel-module implementation (not a portable userspace library), requires modern x86-64 CPU features (AVX/BMI/ADX) with no generic C fallback, and is tightly coupled to the Tempesta FW reverse-proxy project; only covers TLS 1.2/1.3 server handshakes over P-256/x25519.
caveats: This repo (tempesta-tech/tempesta) is already in the run's KNOWN_LIST; reported only under the stated exception because this session located a peer-reviewed workshop paper (Netdev 0x14, 2020) with a fuller benchmark than what was previously catalogued. The win is non-uniform: the large 40-80%/4x figures are for the VM and session-resumption scenarios, while bare-metal new-session throughput improves only 6% alongside much worse tail latency. Compiler flags used to build Nginx/OpenSSL/Tempesta are not stated in the paper.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: HN Algolia search 'faster than openssl' surfaced the story linking to https://netdevconf.info/0x14/pub/papers/35/0x14-paper35-talk-paper.pdf ('Performance study of kernel TLS handshakes', Krizhanovsky & Koveshnikov, Netdev 0x14)
